doc.title: Marty Sheller interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 9, 2022

title: Pricing arrangements and sharing rates with other arrangers
summary: Union minimums, quoting prices, record companies balking then paying later, and telling fellow arrangers about a higher rate.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: How do you charge for arrangements? Is there a union scale, sort of a minimum that you’re supposed to get and as you became more well known could your price for your charts adjust accordingly?

Yes. There is a minimum scale and as time went by and I started getting more recognition, and to be honest the work I was doing — better work — I was more pleased with what I was doing. It got to a point where now when someone calls about an arrangement I’ll ask about the instrumentation, get as much information as I can from them, and then determine about how long it’s going to take me, which by the way I’m not one of those fast arrangers. It takes me some time. And then I just say well my price will be, and that’s the way I get to the price.
How often do people say, oh boy that’s not what I had in mind?

Well I’ll tell you that has happened in my earlier stages. I’ll tell you the story of what would happen. I would give them a price, they would say exactly that, “Well you know the record company’s only paying X amount and they’re not going to go for your price.” So my answer was, “Well sorry about that, maybe we can work again in the future.” And I would say maybe, 95 percent of the time somewhere down the line, a week later or a few days later or so I’d get a call and they would say well we found a way to figure it out, we’re going to put in a certain amount from our pocket so between that and the record company we’ll give you your price.

Yeah. And I also found out that, yeah, I don’t want to mention the names but it was a record company where they were paying a certain price for all arrangements and I felt that it was time for me to get a little more money and I spoke to the fellow who was the person in charge of that, and I said well I’m sorry I can’t do it unless I get that price. And he said to me, “Okay I’ll give you that price but don’t tell any of the other arrangers.” So naturally, you know arrangers are my friends. So the first thing I did I got home and I called them up and I said, “Hey listen, the next arrangement you have, ask for this amount because they gave it to me. You don’t have to mention my name but insist on that.”
Yeah there has to be camaraderie in musicians.
